title: Chapter 2.  History — From Partition's Wound to India's First Planned City

blocks.content: Chandigarh's history is almost entirely a 20th-century story, and that compresses it into a small number of very high-yield facts: the 1947 Partition backdrop, Jawaharlal Nehru's vision, and the sequence of architects (Mayer → Le Corbusier) who designed the city. Nearly every exam question on Chandigarh history touches at least one of these.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The origin of the city stems from the traumatic impact of the 1947 Partition.
The planning and foundational phase of India's first planned city occurred between 1948 and 1953.
Formal milestones were established during its foundation to build a modern capital.
A central political and administrative theme is the ongoing capital dispute between Punjab and Haryana.

blocks.content: Before Chandigarh existed, the land on which it stands comprised 24-odd villages of the erstwhile Punjab (undivided), including the villages of Chandi Mandir (from which the city draws its name) — home to a temple of the goddess Chandi Devi — combined with 'garh' meaning fort/abode, giving 'Chandigarh' the sense of 'the fort/abode of the goddess Chandi'.

The Partition of India in August 1947 split the erstwhile Punjab province into Indian Punjab and Pakistani Punjab. Punjab's historic capital, Lahore, went to Pakistan, leaving the Indian side of Punjab without a capital city — the founding problem that Chandigarh was built to solve.
In the interim (1947–1953), Shimla served as the temporary capital of the Indian Punjab while a new capital was planned and built from scratch.
★ EXAM POINT: 'Why was Chandigarh built?' = Because Partition took Lahore (Punjab's old capital) to Pakistan, leaving Indian Punjab without a capital — Chandigarh was purpose-built to replace Lahore.
From Partition's Wound to India's First Planned City

Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru personally championed the idea of a brand-new, modern planned city — famously describing it as a city 'unfettered by the traditions of the past... an expression of the nation's faith in the future'. This quote is one of the most frequently cited in Chandigarh-related exam material.

The Punjab government first hired the American architect-planner Albert Mayer in 1949 to design the new capital, working with Polish architect Matthew Nowicki. Mayer produced a fan-shaped, curvilinear master plan.

Nowicki's sudden death in a plane crash in 1950 forced the project to find a new lead architect. The commission then passed to the Swiss-French modernist architect Le Corbusier (born Charles-Édouard Jeanneret), who reworked Mayer's plan into the grid-iron layout that defines Chandigarh today.

Le Corbusier was joined by his cousin Pierre Jeanneret and the British husband-and-wife architect team of Maxwell Fry and Jane Drew, who together designed the bulk of the city's residential sectors, schools and civic buildings, while Le Corbusier himself focused on the master plan and the iconic Capitol Complex buildings.

cells: Original 1949–50 fan-shaped master plan; discontinued after Nowicki's death in a 1950 plane crash
Chief architect/planner from 1951; redesigned the master plan into a grid-iron (sectoral) layout; designed the Capitol Complex (Secretariat, High Court, Assembly, Open Hand Monument)
Le Corbusier's cousin and close collaborator; designed extensively across residential sectors and university buildings; lived in Chandigarh for over a decade
British architect couple; designed housing, schools and much of the city's everyday civic fabric

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Sequence to remember: Mayer & Nowicki (fan-shaped plan, 1949–50) → discontinued after Nowicki's death → Le Corbusier takes over (1951) and redesigns it as a GRID-IRON plan, assisted by Pierre Jeanneret, Maxwell Fry and Jane Drew.

cells: Punjab government decides to build a new capital; site near the village of Chandigarh selected
Albert Mayer & Matthew Nowicki commissioned; initial fan-shaped master plan prepared
Nowicki dies in a plane crash; project reassigned
Le Corbusier appointed chief architect; grid-iron master plan adopted
Foundation-stone laying / first construction of the Capitol Complex begins
Chandigarh formally becomes the capital of the (undivided) Indian Punjab, replacing Shimla as interim capital

Under the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966, Punjab is bifurcated into Punjab and Haryana on linguistic lines; Chandigarh is carved out as a separate Union Territory administered by the Centre, and designated the joint capital of both new states

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: 1 November 1966 is the single most important date in this chapter — the Punjab Reorganisation Act created Haryana out of Punjab and simultaneously made Chandigarh a Union Territory serving as the shared capital of both.

items: Exams frequently ask about the initial planning and foundation timeline (1948–1953) of India's first planned city.
Focus on the political and historical background of the Punjab–Haryana capital dispute following state reorganization.

blocks.content: Since 1966, the question of which state Chandigarh should 'belong' to has remained a live political issue. The Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973) by the Akali Dal and subsequent Punjab-side demands sought Chandigarh's transfer wholly to Punjab, arguing that as the historic capital built on land acquired mostly from Punjabi villages, it should be Punjab's alone.

In 1985, the Rajiv Gandhi–Longowal Accord (Punjab Accord) proposed transferring Chandigarh to Punjab by 26 January 1986, with some Hindi-speaking areas of Punjab going to Haryana in compensation — but the transfer was never implemented and the dispute remains unresolved to this day, making Chandigarh's status a long-running Centre-State relations case study frequently referenced in polity and current-affairs material.

items: Name origin: 'Chandigarh' from the Chandi Mandir temple (goddess Chandi) + 'garh' (fort/abode).
Built because Partition (1947) gave Lahore, Punjab's old capital, to Pakistan; Shimla served as interim capital 1947–53.
Nehru called it a city 'unfettered by the traditions of the past'.
Planners: Albert Mayer & Matthew Nowicki (fan-shaped plan) → Le Corbusier (grid-iron plan, from 1951), with Pierre Jeanneret, Maxwell Fry & Jane Drew.
1 November 1966: Punjab Reorganisation Act creates Haryana; Chandigarh becomes a separate UT and joint capital of Punjab & Haryana.
1985 Rajiv Gandhi–Longowal Accord proposed transferring Chandigarh to Punjab by 26 Jan 1986 — never implemented; the dispute is still unresolved.
